question: Are flat Euclidean representations a fundamental bottleneck for foundation models, and do metric-embedding theory, synthetic distortion experiments, and descriptive LLM token geometry justify making hyperbolic, spherical, mixed-curvature, or dynamically selected manifolds a core part of billion-parameter models?

key_findings.claim: The paper articulates an ambitious and useful research program, but its strongest wording—non-Euclidean foundation models are essential to maintain scaling laws—is a position rather than a conclusion supported by its experiments.
key_findings.evidence: The proposed benefits are representational efficiency, task-aware adaptability, and continued scaling, with suggested paths through geometric fine-tuning, from-scratch pretraining, and hybrid architectures. Yet the paper trains no language, vision, or multimodal foundation model, fits no loss-versus-compute scaling law, and measures no hallucination, task accuracy, throughput, or parameter-efficiency outcome. It later explicitly says that no conclusive study connects embedding distortion to downstream foundation-model performance.

anchors.section: Position, Representational Capabilities, Adaptability, and Scalability

key_findings.claim: The distinction between local Riemannian isometry and global metric-space isometry is correct and prevents a common misuse of the Nash embedding theorem.
key_findings.evidence: An isometric immersion or embedding preserves the tangent metric and therefore curve lengths, but Euclidean chord distance between embedded points need not equal the manifold's intrinsic shortest-path distance. The sphere-in-Euclidean-space example correctly shows why Nash does not guarantee a finite-dimensional Euclidean representation that preserves all intrinsic pairwise distances under ordinary Euclidean distance.

anchors.section: 3.1 Non-Applicability of the Nash Embedding Theorem

key_findings.claim: The paper incorrectly extends a Euclidean dimension lower bound for the uniform complete-graph metric to every unweighted graph.
key_findings.evidence: Theorem 3.1 concerns an n-point metric with every non-identical pair at distance one. The text then says any unweighted graph can be isometrically embedded into an unweighted complete graph on the same n nodes and therefore inherits the same dimensionality issue. This is false for shortest-path metrics: a non-complete graph has pairs at distance greater than one, whereas an unweighted complete graph makes every pair distance one. The theorem is still relevant as a worst-case finite metric example, but not as a universal implication for all graphs.

key_findings.claim: Metric-embedding lower bounds establish representational trade-offs for specified target distances, not a universal performance ceiling for Euclidean Transformers.
key_findings.evidence: Theorems 3.2-3.3 concern bi-Lipschitz preservation of a chosen graph or manifold metric by one embedding and standard Euclidean distance. Foundation models are not required to preserve every shortest-path distance among tokens: they learn task-dependent inner products, nonlinear layerwise features, attention kernels, and decoders. The paper never defines the ground-truth token metric whose global isometry is necessary, nor proves that representation distortion upper-bounds prediction loss. Its step from metric distortion to a downstream performance bottleneck is therefore an unproven modeling assumption.

key_findings.claim: The synthetic 96-node experiments support the narrow proposition that matching curvature to a known canonical metric reduces embedding distortion at low dimension.
key_findings.evidence: At total dimension six, Euclidean, hyperbolic, spherical, and hyperbolic-times-spherical spaces are fitted to a tree, cycle, and ring of trees. The best average point-wise distortions match intuition: hyperbolic 0.0454 for the tree versus Euclidean 0.1036; spherical 0.0011 for the cycle versus Euclidean 0.1042; and product geometry 0.0686 for the ring of trees versus Euclidean 0.1060. Dimension sweeps visually show Euclidean plateaus and lower non-Euclidean distortion.

key_findings.claim: The synthetic embedding evidence is too small and under-specified to validate foundation-model scalability or even permit exact replication.
key_findings.evidence: All three graphs contain only 96 nodes, and the paper supplies final distortion numbers and plots without an optimization objective beyond the reported point-wise statistic, algorithm, initialization, learning rate, iteration budget, number of runs, seed, uncertainty, code link, or train/test split. It compares directly optimized coordinates in spaces chosen with prior knowledge of each graph, not learned end-to-end representations inside a transformer. No wall-clock, numerical-stability, or dimension-versus-compute comparison is made.

key_findings.claim: The reported delta-hyperbolicity values do not, as documented, establish comparable tree geometry across models or datasets.
key_findings.evidence: Table 1 reports values roughly 0.07-0.20 for RoBERTa, LLaMA-3.1-8B, GPT-NeoX-20B, and Gemma-2-9B and compares them with sphere 0.99, dense graph 0.62-0.63, PubMed 0.40, Poincare 0.14, and tree 0. The appendix defines raw delta but does not specify distance normalization. Delta has units and scales linearly with all distances, so arbitrary embedding rescaling can make it arbitrarily small. The construction from token similarity to a graph, edge weighting, threshold or neighborhood size, prompt sampling, four-point sampling, normalization, and uncertainty source are also absent. Raw values across unrelated metric spaces are therefore not interpretable as a calibrated hierarchy score.

key_findings.claim: Zipf-like token frequencies and embedding-norm histograms do not by themselves identify a hyperbolic latent metric or a Euclidean failure.
key_findings.evidence: The paper observes power-law token counts and links scale-free frequency to hierarchy, then notes that embedding-norm counts only partly resemble the frequency distribution and fall at the right tail. Token frequency is determined by corpus, tokenizer, and lexical Zipf effects rather than pairwise embedding geometry; many Euclidean mechanisms can encode frequency in norms. No power-law fit, alternative distribution, correlation coefficient, controlled tokenizer/corpus comparison, or test that a hyperbolic model better reproduces the distribution is reported.

key_findings.claim: The paper's attention argument does not prove that Euclidean attention is unable to represent the claimed relationships.
key_findings.evidence: Lemma 3.4 bounds one attention head's output by the convex hull of transformed previous tokens, but the paper then jumps from descriptive token hyperbolicity to the conclusion that dot-product attention cannot faithfully capture hierarchy, cycles, or long-range dependencies. The lemma contains no curvature or distortion term and does not compare the expressivity of multi-head, multi-layer Euclidean and manifold attention. Hyperbolic distance is a plausible inductive bias, not a necessity established by that result.

key_findings.claim: The roadmap is the paper's strongest contribution because it decomposes a vague geometric-foundation-model goal into three build paths and concrete modules.
key_findings.evidence: For existing models it proposes geometric prompt tuning, manifold LoRA, geometric distillation, and geometry-aligned transfer. For pretraining it identifies curvature estimation, distance-based attention, positional encoding, residuals, normalization, loss, and Riemannian optimization. Hybrid designs combine product manifolds, geometry-aware mixtures of experts, and multi-manifold attention so geometry can vary by input or task.

key_findings.claim: Table 4 is an illustrative menu rather than a general mathematical specification for non-Euclidean foundation models.
key_findings.evidence: A scalar K describes only constant-curvature factors, not an arbitrary or spatially varying Riemannian geometry. Parallel transport is path-dependent on curved manifolds and is not automatically a RoPE replacement; Frechet means can be non-unique; log maps have cut-locus/domain issues; exp-map residuals require tangent vectors at the correct base point; and Mobius FFNs are hyperbolic-specific. Squared-distance attention also does not reduce to dot-product attention at K=0 without norm constraints. These choices need manifold-specific well-posedness, expressivity, and stability proofs rather than a universal substitution table.

anchors.section: 4.2 Non-Euclidean Attention and Other Important Modules

key_findings.claim: The paper candidly identifies the decisive engineering and causal-evidence gaps, but answers them only with hypotheses.
key_findings.evidence: It notes expensive tangent mappings, slower manifold operations, need for optimized libraries and distributed kernels, and the lack of a conclusive distortion-to-performance link. The proposed counterargument is that reduced dimension might offset overhead, but there are no throughput, memory, communication, mixed-precision, stability, or end-to-end compute measurements. Claims that geometry could mitigate hallucination or continue scaling remain explicitly future research.

anchors.section: Learning Inductive Bias with Euclidean Models

method.core_idea: Make the case that the geometry of representations and neural operations should match hierarchical, cyclical, symmetric, multimodal, and mixed-curvature structure instead of defaulting to a globally flat latent space; then supply a research roadmap from parameter-efficient adaptation to fully manifold-native foundation models.
method.mechanism: Review Riemannian and metric-embedding theory to motivate low-distortion curved representations; directly optimize embeddings of a tree, cycle, and ring-of-trees in Euclidean, hyperbolic, spherical, and product spaces; diagnose existing token embeddings with raw delta-hyperbolicity, token-frequency, and norm distributions; connect these observations to attention and multimodal representation arguments; and enumerate geometric versions of prompt tuning, LoRA, distillation, transfer, curvature estimation, attention, positional encoding, residuals, normalization, losses, optimization, FFNs, and mixture-of-geometry routing.
assumptions: Foundation-model representations must approximately preserve a well-defined real-world metric globally, rather than only information needed for prediction or generation.
The relevant target metric for tokens, images, modalities, or scientific data is known or can be reliably estimated from observations.
Metric-embedding distortion causally limits downstream loss, reasoning, hallucination, transfer, or sample efficiency.
Worst-case lower bounds for particular finite metrics describe the learned representations and tasks encountered by foundation models.
Low-dimensional synthetic graph embeddings predict the behavior of billion- or trillion-parameter end-to-end networks.
The graph built from token similarities is stable to similarity function, threshold, k-nearest-neighbor choice, layer, context, and corpus.
Raw delta-hyperbolicity is normalized or otherwise comparable across metric spaces with different scales and diameters.
Zipf-like token frequency implies hierarchical pairwise geometry rather than a corpus/tokenizer frequency law.
Embedding norms should reproduce token-frequency counts, and deviation at one histogram tail diagnoses insufficient Euclidean expressivity.
A curved metric's representational efficiency survives optimization error, finite precision, boundary effects, and the cost of manifold operations.
One or a small product of constant-curvature manifolds adequately models heterogeneous, local, and task-dependent geometry.
Geometry-specific attention, residual, normalization, and FFN replacements retain or improve the expressivity and trainability of modern Transformer blocks.
Learned geometry routing will specialize meaningfully instead of collapsing, duplicating experts, or exploiting scale differences among branches.
Parameter count or embedding dimension is the relevant efficiency measure even when curved operations have different FLOPs, memory traffic, and hardware utilization.
Benefits shown for equivariance, graph models, or metric learning transfer to general-purpose autoregressive foundation models.

techniques.role: Separates global pairwise-distance preservation from the local tangent-metric preservation guaranteed by Nash-style embeddings.
Uses finite-metric and Markov-convexity results to motivate Euclidean dimension and distortion limits.
Compares optimized low-dimensional coordinates for a tree, cycle, and ring of trees across flat, negative-, positive-, and mixed-curvature spaces.
Treats tokens as points in a similarity-derived metric graph and estimates how tree-like the resulting space is.
Compares Zipf-like corpus token counts with learned embedding-norm histograms as qualitative evidence for scale-free structure.
Proposes manifold-valued prompt tokens and low-rank updates for adapting Euclidean foundation models.
Preserves teacher or cross-domain structural relations through geometry-alignment objectives.
Selects or learns graph, text, and image curvature through topological statistics, embeddings, self-supervision, or routing.
Replaces query-key dot products with negative geodesic distances and aggregates values by tangent-space or Frechet-mean operations.
Recasts positional encoding, residuals, normalization, loss, optimization, and FFNs with parallel transport, exp/log maps, retractions, and Mobius operations.
Combines Euclidean, spherical, and hyperbolic factors to represent datasets with several geometric signatures.
Routes inputs or components toward curvature-specific experts so the representation geometry can vary dynamically.
Computes parallel attention maps in several geometries and fuses them for heterogeneous relations.

evaluations.setting: Canonical 96-node tree, cycle, and ring-of-trees metrics embedded at total dimension six.
evaluations.result: Tree: Euclidean 0.1036, hyperbolic 0.0454, spherical 0.1440, product 0.0624. Cycle: Euclidean 0.1042, hyperbolic 0.2356, spherical 0.0011, product 0.1337. Ring of trees: Euclidean 0.1060, hyperbolic 0.0736, spherical 0.1365, product 0.0686.
evaluations.baseline: Equal reported intrinsic dimension in Euclidean R^6, hyperbolic H^{-1,6}, spherical S^{1,6}, and H^{-1,3}×S^{1,3}; fitting protocol and uncertainty are not reported.

evaluations.setting: Dimension sweeps for the same three 96-node canonical graphs.
evaluations.metric: Average point-wise distortion versus embedding dimension on a log scale.
evaluations.result: The figures show Euclidean curves plateauing while matched-curvature spaces attain lower distortion; for the tree, a four-dimensional hyperbolic embedding is stated to beat a 50-dimensional Euclidean embedding.
evaluations.baseline: Directly optimized Euclidean, fixed-curvature, and half-hyperbolic/half-spherical coordinates; no compute, seed, or convergence comparison.

evaluations.setting: Token embeddings from RoBERTa-Base, LLaMA-3.1-8B, GPT-NeoX-20B, and Gemma-2-9B across arXiv, C4, Common Crawl, GitHub, StackExchange, and Wikipedia subsets.
evaluations.metric: Raw delta-hyperbolicity of a graph constructed from pairwise token similarities.
evaluations.result: Reported means range from 0.07 to 0.20 and are interpreted as tree-like by comparison with Poincare 0.14 and tree 0; scale normalization, graph construction, sample count, and uncertainty source are not supplied.
evaluations.baseline: Reference sphere 0.99, dense graph about 0.62-0.63, PubMed 0.40, Poincare 0.14, and tree 0.

evaluations.setting: Corpus/token embedding statistics for GPT-NeoX-20B, OPT-13B, RoBERTa-Base, Gemma-2-9B, LLaMA-3.1-8B, LLaMA-13B, and a visual generator.
evaluations.metric: Log-scale token-frequency counts and histograms of token counts by embedding norm.
evaluations.result: Frequency follows a visually power-law-like decay; norm histograms rise at the low-norm tail and fall at high norms. The authors interpret partial resemblance as learned scale-free structure and the high-norm fall as incomplete Euclidean capture, without fitted exponents or statistical tests.
evaluations.baseline: A qualitative expectation that embedding-norm counts should track corpus frequency and that hyperbolic embeddings would do so more faithfully; no non-Euclidean model is evaluated.

evaluations.setting: Foundation-model performance, scaling, hallucination, and systems claims.
evaluations.metric: Downstream loss/accuracy, scaling exponent, parameter or token efficiency, throughput, memory, and calibration/hallucination rate.
evaluations.result: No measurements are reported; the paper explicitly identifies the distortion-performance link as unresolved future work.
evaluations.baseline: Matched Euclidean and non-Euclidean foundation models over model size, data, compute, and wall-clock budgets.

limitations: [Author-stated, p. 9-10] Manifold maps and operations add engineering overhead, and existing distributed and accelerated training libraries are designed for Euclidean kernels.
[Author-stated, p. 10] No conclusive study links embedding distortion directly to downstream foundation-model performance.
[Author-stated, p. 10] Euclidean models may learn structural inductive biases from scale, data augmentation, and data quality rather than hard-coding geometry.
[Reviewer-identified] The paper trains no non-Euclidean foundation model, so its necessity, scaling-law, hallucination, and efficiency claims are untested in the work itself.
[Reviewer-identified] Theorem 3.1 is incorrectly generalized from a uniform complete-graph metric to every unweighted graph.
[Reviewer-identified] Metric-embedding bounds require a target distance and isometry objective that the paper never defines for language or multimodal prediction.
[Reviewer-identified] The jump from representation distortion to a downstream performance upper bound has no theorem or causal experiment.
[Reviewer-identified] Synthetic experiments contain only 96 nodes, known geometry, and direct coordinate fitting; they are not foundation-model experiments.
[Reviewer-identified] Graph fitting omits optimizer, initialization, seeds, repetitions, convergence, uncertainty, and code, limiting reproducibility.
[Reviewer-identified] Raw delta-hyperbolicity is scale-sensitive, yet no diameter normalization or common metric scale is documented.
[Reviewer-identified] Token similarity graph construction, edge weighting, threshold/k, layer, context, sample count, and four-point estimation protocol are unspecified.
[Reviewer-identified] Token-frequency and norm plots receive no fitted power law, goodness-of-fit, competing distribution, correlation, or controlled tokenizer analysis.
[Reviewer-identified] Zipf frequency is not a measurement of pairwise semantic curvature and can arise independently of representation geometry.
[Reviewer-identified] The attention convex-hull lemma does not prove a limitation specific to Euclidean geometry.

[Reviewer-identified] Equivariance and curved latent metrics are conceptually distinct; Euclidean-coordinate architectures can encode group equivariance without using a non-Euclidean embedding distance.
[Reviewer-identified] Table 4 conflates generic Riemannian operations, constant-curvature product spaces, and specifically hyperbolic Mobius algebra.
[Reviewer-identified] Non-uniqueness of Frechet means, cut loci, parallel-transport path dependence, curvature routing, and finite-precision boundary instability are not addressed.
[Reviewer-identified] Equal parameter count, equal embedding dimension, equal nominal FLOPs, and equal wall time are different comparison regimes, but no evaluation protocol is specified for them.
failure_modes: Choosing hyperbolic geometry because a dataset contains some hierarchy can harm cyclical, dense, local-Euclidean, or mixed relations in the same data.
A learnable curvature parameter can collapse toward zero, run to a numerically unstable extreme, or act as an unidentifiable rescaling of embeddings and temperature.
Mixture-of-geometry routing can collapse to one branch, split by superficial scale, or duplicate experts without learning meaningful geometric specialization.
Poincare embeddings near the boundary suffer exploding distances, vanishing or unstable gradients, and reduced effective precision at high dimension.
Repeated exp/log maps can accumulate error and erase the theoretical information-compression advantage through extra memory traffic and low hardware utilization.
Frechet-mean aggregation can be non-unique, iterative, or costly and can introduce discontinuities when the selected minimizer changes.
Parallel transport used as positional encoding depends on a chosen path and connection; an inconsistent choice can destroy relative-position identities.
A metric chosen to minimize graph distortion may optimize irrelevant relations and reduce downstream task accuracy even when its geometric score improves.
Unnormalized delta-hyperbolicity can be made small by rescaling embeddings, allowing a model to appear more tree-like without any structural change.
A similarity-to-graph threshold can manufacture tree-like sparsity, making the diagnostic reflect preprocessing rather than hidden-state geometry.
Token-frequency effects can be mistaken for hierarchy, causing geometry selection to track corpus frequency rather than semantics or syntax.
Nominal parameter savings can be overwhelmed by expensive distance, transcendental, retraction, communication, and manifold-normalization kernels.
A fixed constant-curvature geometry can be less expressive than a high-dimensional Euclidean model for tasks whose useful metric changes across layers or contexts.

Using a stronger geometry-specific architecture against an under-tuned Euclidean baseline can attribute gains to curvature that actually come from parameterization, normalization, routing, or regularization.
reusable_insights: Distinguish the coordinate space, the metric used by the loss or attention, the symmetry group encoded by the architecture, and the intrinsic geometry inferred from data; these are related but not interchangeable.
Treat geometry selection as a falsifiable model-selection problem with Euclidean, fixed-curvature, product, and learned-mixture controls rather than assuming curved is always better.
Normalize scale-dependent geometry statistics by diameter or another explicit scale and publish the exact similarity-to-metric construction.
Validate the causal chain separately: target structure to measured geometry, geometry to distortion, distortion to task behavior, and task behavior to compute or sample efficiency.
Compare models at matched parameters, nominal FLOPs, training tokens, wall-clock time, peak memory, and energy because geometry can change each axis differently.
Use synthetic canonical spaces as unit tests for implementations, not as substitutes for end-to-end foundation-model evidence.
The three-path roadmap—adapt existing models, pretrain manifold-native models, and build geometry mixtures—is a useful modular decomposition for engineering and ablation.
A geometry-aware mixture should include a zero-curvature expert and diagnostics for routing entropy, curvature identifiability, specialization, and collapse.
Design manifold modules to recover a known Euclidean architecture continuously at zero curvature; this provides a strong correctness test and nested baseline.
Pair representational diagnostics with task interventions: deliberately reduce distortion while holding architecture and compute fixed, then test whether prediction changes as hypothesized.
Report numerical-domain margins, exp/log conditioning, invalid-value rates, precision sensitivity, and distributed-kernel throughput alongside accuracy.
Subsequent billion-scale hyperbolic models make the agenda empirically testable, but one favorable model comparison is evidence for a contingent inductive bias, not proof of geometric necessity.
open_questions: What ground-truth or task-induced metric should a language model preserve, and is global pairwise isometry actually necessary for next-token prediction?
Does normalized hidden-state hyperbolicity predict which tasks, layers, contexts, or examples benefit from a hyperbolic intervention?
Can changing distortion alone, through a controlled regularizer or representation reparameterization, causally change downstream loss while compute and capacity remain fixed?
Do hyperbolic or mixed-curvature LLMs change the scaling exponent, or only the loss prefactor, under matched tokens, FLOPs, wall time, memory, and optimized kernels?
At what model size or embedding dimension do numerical and systems costs outweigh lower geometric distortion?
Can a zero-curvature limit make all manifold modules exactly recover a standard Transformer, enabling nested statistical comparisons?
How should local, layer-dependent, token-dependent, or task-dependent curvature be estimated without leakage from downstream labels?
Can geometry mixtures avoid routing collapse and learn stable, interpretable specializations beyond frequency and embedding norm?
Are gains from hyperbolic attention caused by curvature, distance-based kernels, norm constraints, hard-negative behavior, regularization, or architectural changes?
How do learned curved models compare with Euclidean group-equivariant models and data augmentation when the relevant structure is symmetry rather than hierarchy?
Can manifold-native attention, normalization, residuals, and FFNs be fused into efficient mixed-precision GPU kernels with competitive throughput at multi-node scale?
Which benchmark suite jointly measures hierarchy, cycles, symmetry, heterogeneous modality geometry, ordinary language quality, stability, and real compute cost?
Do geometry-aware models reduce hallucination or improve calibration after controlling for accuracy and capacity, and what mechanistic link would explain that effect?
Can tokenization itself be made geometry-aware, or does a discrete vocabulary impose frequency artifacts that dominate embedding diagnostics?

competitive_landscape.title: Geometric Deep Learning: Grids, Groups, Graphs, Geodesics, and Gauges
competitive_landscape.difference: Bronstein et al. organize geometric inductive bias around domains and symmetry groups across grids, graphs, manifolds, and gauges. This broader blueprint shows that going beyond generic Euclidean models need not mean putting every hidden state on a constant-curvature manifold; equivariance, locality, and gauge structure can be encoded in Euclidean-coordinate tensors. The position paper narrows attention toward latent metrics and manifold-native modules at foundation-model scale.

competitive_landscape.title: Fully Hyperbolic Neural Networks
competitive_landscape.difference: Chen et al. build Lorentz transformations and neural operations that stay in hyperbolic space instead of repeatedly using the origin tangent space, with gains on four NLP tasks. It supplies important concrete module machinery predating the roadmap, but its shallow/deep task models are far below modern foundation-model scale and do not establish scaling-law changes.

competitive_landscape.title: Hyperbolic Image-Text Representations
competitive_landscape.difference: MERU trains a contrastive image-text model whose hyperbolic space explicitly represents entailment and reports structured, interpretable representations competitive with CLIP on classification and retrieval. It is a stronger end-to-end multimodal demonstration than the position paper's synthetic fits, while also showing that hierarchy benefits can be evaluated without replacing every network operation with a manifold counterpart.

competitive_landscape.title: Curve Your Attention: Mixed-Curvature Transformers for Graph Representation Learning
competitive_landscape.difference: Cho et al. implement a fully product-stereographic Transformer with end-to-end curvature learning and kernelized linear-complexity attention, then test graph reconstruction and node classification. It directly instantiates the product-manifold and learnable-curvature ideas in the roadmap, but on graph tasks rather than general-purpose foundation-model pretraining.

competitive_landscape.title: Hyperbolic vs Euclidean Embeddings in Few-Shot Learning: Two Sides of the Same Coin
competitive_landscape.difference: Moreira et al. trace hyperbolic few-shot gains to embeddings converging toward a common radius and show a fixed-radius Euclidean encoder can do better regardless of dimension. This is a crucial competing explanation: apparent curvature benefits may arise from norm constraints or regularization, so comparisons must isolate geometry from the induced representation distribution.

competitive_landscape.title: Why are hyperbolic neural networks effective? A study on hierarchical representation capability
competitive_landscape.difference: Tan et al. argue that theoretical existence of a low-distortion hyperbolic embedding does not imply trained HNNs find it; their benchmark reports that HNNs fail to attain the theoretical optimum and that objectives and hierarchy-aware pretraining drive representation quality. This directly qualifies the position paper's inference from embedding existence theorems to trained model capability.

competitive_landscape.title: Hyperbolic Fine-Tuning for Large Language Models
competitive_landscape.difference: HypLoRA performs low-rank adaptation directly on a hyperbolic manifold and reports reasoning gains across several base models while studying token frequency and hyperbolicity. It operationalizes the position paper's most feasible near-term route, but remains a downstream fine-tuning intervention and shares the need to separate hyperbolicity diagnostics from causal geometry benefits.

competitive_landscape.title: Does equivariance matter at scale?
competitive_landscape.difference: Brehmer et al. actually vary model size, training length, data, and compute for equivariant and general-purpose Transformers. Equivariance improves data efficiency and lowers loss at tested compute budgets, while augmentation closes the small-data gap; both remain power laws with compatible compute exponents but different prefactors and optimal allocations. This is the type of controlled scaling study the position paper calls for and cautions that structure may improve constants rather than 'maintain' an otherwise failing scaling law.

competitive_landscape.title: HyperCore: The Core Framework for Building Hyperbolic Foundation Models with Comprehensive Modules
competitive_landscape.difference: Submitted minutes after the position paper by overlapping authors, HyperCore supplies the missing reusable module library and constructs Lorentz ViT, hyperbolic CLIP, and hyperbolic GraphRAG examples, plus reproduction benchmarks. It converts part of the engineering roadmap into code and end-to-end models, though its reported experiments are demonstrations rather than a broad compute-matched foundation-model scaling analysis.

competitive_landscape.title: HELM: Hyperbolic Large Language Models via Mixture-of-Curvature Experts
competitive_landscape.difference: HELM is the clearest subsequent test of the roadmap: it adds hyperbolic positional encoding, RMS normalization, latent attention, dense and mixture-of-curvature experts, trains fully hyperbolic LLMs at billion-parameter scale, and reports gains up to four percent over LLaMA/DeepSeek-style Euclidean architectures. This materially strengthens feasibility after the position paper, but one size range and architecture family still do not prove geometric necessity, changed asymptotic scaling, or wall-clock superiority.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The paper claims that billion-parameter non-Euclidean foundation models are necessary for representational fidelity, adaptability, and continued scaling, and proposes a comprehensive roadmap spanning adaptation, from-scratch pretraining, and hybrid geometry-aware systems.
novelty_assessment.evidence: It combines metric-embedding theory, small canonical graph fits, descriptive token hyperbolicity/frequency diagnostics, a broad literature synthesis, and an operation-by-operation architecture table. Its distinctive contribution is framing previously fragmented hyperbolic, spherical, equivariant, and mixed-curvature techniques as one foundation-model-scale agenda.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The synthesis and modular roadmap are valuable, and subsequent HyperCore/HELM work shows that the agenda is technically feasible. The paper itself does not demonstrate necessity, scaling-law continuation, hallucination reduction, or net efficiency; one theorem is overgeneralized incorrectly and the token-geometry evidence is not reproducibly or scale-invariantly specified. The most defensible novelty is a field-organizing position plus research checklist, not a validated empirical or theoretical result about foundation-model performance.

reviewer_notes: Read all 27 pages of current arXiv v2 / LoG 2025 version, including theoretical statements, all main experiments, alternative views, appendices on isometry and Markov convexity, data/statistics details, delta-hyperbolicity definition, and geometric operation table; reference-only pages were also scanned. Current competitive research was checked on 2026-08-23 using primary arXiv records, with special attention to controlled counterevidence, the authors' same-day HyperCore companion, and their later billion-scale HELM result. Exact target-paper numerical claims are drawn from the extracted full text; deductions about scale dependence, theorem scope, and missing causal links are labeled as reviewer audits.
